title: The rate call that came late
intro: Dynamic bond funds promise to time the rate cycle for you. The cycle just completed — open the duration data and judge the promise.

facts.label: The mandate
facts.value: Dynamic bond funds may move across maturities freely — long when rates should fall, short when they should rise. Timing is the entire pitch.

facts.label: The duration record
facts.value: The category's median duration was modest as yields peaked — and ROSE only after the 10-year yield had already started coming down, touching over eight years late in the move.

facts.label: The yield path
facts.value: The 10-year bottomed at 6.2% by May 2025 — the big duration gains belonged to positions taken before the fall, not after it began.

facts.label: The outcome
facts.value: The typical fund caught part of the bond rally. Not the early part.

facts.label: The incentive
facts.value: Extending duration early is visibly wrong if the view stalls; extending after confirmation is career-safe.

question: What does the duration record show?
choices: Managers called the cycle early and captured the full rally
Duration rose only after yields had begun falling — flexibility was used to follow the rally, not front-run it
Dynamic funds never changed duration at all
debrief: The pattern is unambiguous: duration extended after the yield decline was underway and peaked late in the move — confirmation-following, not foresight. The funds still caught part of the rally (following works, partially), but the premium you pay for a timing mandate bought reactive positioning. The rhyme with the SIF cover story is the issue's real thesis: mandate freedom — shorting, duration, going anywhere — is capacity, not clairvoyance. Audit *when* a flexible fund moved, not whether it eventually did; and if you hold a rate view, own it directly or hold bonds for carry.
